newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Tunisia deal kicks off new barley season.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Tunisia deal kicks off new barley season.

text.p: Next season's world barley price, one of the most speculative in slippery grain markets, took greater shape on Friday when Tunisia became the first importer to buy exclusively from this year's crop, traders said.
The North African buyer bought 100,000 tonnes in four shipments between September and November at $136.72 per tonne including freight on the international market, exporters said.
The deal, for barley of optional origin, is said to work out at approximately $120 per tonne Fob if the grain ends up being shipped from the European Union, the world's leading exporter.
That is some $9-10 a tonne less than the going rate for last year's crop sold with EU subsidies now standing at $37 a tonne.
But although the EU could well be a supplier, purchase terms also leave room for South Africa, a more marginal supplier recently seen offering feed barley while buying malting grades.
Other main contenders to supply the deal include the United States, Russia and Canada, trade experts said.
Several traders said the deal's price looked competitive, but warned it was too early to have more than a hunch at this stage. Others called it a reasonable bet for the seller.
"You really can't be sure what the barley world price is going to be doing in five or six months' time. Right now all you can do is take a view and make an offer," one trader said.
Domestic prices are not yet quoted in Europe for barley this autumn and in any case would hardly get a look in during the composition of a world market deal several months forward.
"You just have to trade on your best view of what the dollar world market will be doing - full stop," another trader said.
Judging by bids that went into the Tunisian purchase tender, however, few companies have the same ideas.
Although two were said to have picked a number within a few cents of each other, lowest and highest offers were seen up to $17 per tonne apart, seven percent of the final price.

Traders reported offers for the barley and freight as high as $151.67 per tonne, while one operator tried for some $150, others in the mid $140s and others still around $138 to $139. It was not clear what, if any, conditions each offer laid down.

Although the EU is the dominant player depending on the time of year and exporters' logistics, competition for the autumn shipment period should be thrust wide open, traders said. Some had offered to sell surplus Turkish or Syrian barley.
Friday's sale was the first exclusively for new-crop barley, following a combined sale from both harvests to Tunisia at very nearly the same price earlier this year.

For old-crop barley, however, the market remained firmly focused on the timing of any new purchase by Saudi Arabia. Analysts have said this could be a million tonnes, though some traders doubt Riyadh will offer up such a large bonanza.
Operators said they did not see the world's largest feed barley importer in the market before the beginning of May, with the Eid al-Adha holiday tentatively due to start on April 13.
"If they don't come in next week you won't see them before the beginning of May," one trader commented.

The kingdom, a shrewd buyer with annual needs of around five million tonnes, appears covered up to May and will want to rely on surpluses nearer to home while waiting for the market to crowd up again with sellers, a European trade expert predicted.
